analysis: Documentation-only units examined. docs/developer/test.md head 767-790 adds an 'Add-On Hold' test section: AF_UNIX socket at a private temp runtime dir, flock ownership lock, peer policy exercised only negatively (test authenticator substitutes for the signed add-on), drain/unload/lease/reconnect coverage, and 503 draining rejection. docs/provider/cli-reference.md head 156 and 904-932 documents the new `darkbloom addon` status/hold/release(--force) commands, which reach the provider via an owner-only lifecycle mailbox bound to the live process identity. Head 1758 documents the runtime dir ~/.darkbloom/runtime (0700) with addon.sock and addon-hold.json (0600), plus the DARKBLOOM_ADDON_SOCKET test override. This introduces a new local IPC surface (add-on socket and peer authentication) not described in the canonical threat model. TB-003 (operator vs process) and TB-010 (privileged helper) cover analogous local IPC but not the add-on hold. The documented behavior is an availability control: it unloads models and closes admission. It is operator-controllable by design, so no confidentiality or attestation impact is established from the docs; the operator already controls availability (T-016-like). Integration questions remain: (1) Whether the actual implementation (AddonIPCServer, AddonPeerPolicy, AddonHoldPaths, ProviderLoop+AddonHold.swift) enforces code-signing peer checks. It must also confirm that the DARKBLOOM_ADDON_SOCKET override is test-only in release builds. (2) Whether a hold or drain heartbeat with busy fields could affect coordinator routing or billing, including the 503 draining rejection. (3) The threat model should add a trust boundary/threat for local add-on IPC (spoofed peer forcing unload/DoS, stale socket takeover). No source was supplied, so these remain coverage limits rather than findings. No changes to the cache (T-041) or the attestation/logout sections were observed; those sections are unchanged text.
